newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil hosts Americas free trade talking shop.
newsitem.headline: Brazil hosts Americas free trade talking shop.

text.p: Trade ministers from across the Americas meet in the Brazilian industrial city of Belo Horizonte this week to hammer out a deal on setting up a free trade zone from Alaska to the plains of Patagonian.

Diplomats said the battle lines are clearly drawn, halfway between Brasilia and Washington, as the northern superpower and South America's Mercosur trade bloc wrestle over who will influence the Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) the most.
"Relations between Brazil and the United States are very good," said Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso during a visit to Uruguay recently.

"But that does not mean Brazil and Mercosur can give themselves the luxury of not looking after their own interests," said Cardoso, whose country is the industrial power of the four-nation bloc, also grouping Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.
Leaders of 34 countries in the Americas, excluding Cuba's Fidel Castro, agreed at the 1994 Miami summit to set up a free trade zone of 1 billion potential consumers by the year 2005.
At Belo Horizonte, the third summit of trade ministers since Miami and which runs from May 14-16, participants were expected to map out the structure and timetable of formal negotiations.
All agree talks ought to begin after a presidential summit in Santiago, Chile, next March, Brazilian officials said.

But Washington, backed by Canada, wants to discuss everything from tariff-reductions to subsidies at the same time. Brazil is demanding more structured talks, with tariff reductions preferably left till last.
Diplomats said the core problem was a Brazilian fear of rapid market opening to competitive U.S. products just after the "shock" of liberalizing trade over the past three years.
Brazil believes its efforts have not been met by a similar readiness in Washington to reduce non-tariff barriers blocking Brazilian orange juice and steel exports.

"Brazilian industry was submitted to an intense competitive shock. But this did not meet a corresponding increase in access to markets where our products face restrictions," Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia has repeatedly argued.
Brazil's trade balance has deteriorated drastically from 1994's $10 billion surplus to a $5.5 billion deficit last year, with most estimates pointing to a $12 billion gap in 1997.

The other element determining Brazil's stance is the success of the Mercosur trade bloc, which has struck associate deals with Chile and Bolivia and is discussing deals with a host of other countries, including Canada and the European Union.
"Our priority is to strengthen Mercosur and expand it," said a high-ranking Brazilian diplomat, requesting anonymity.
The fiery Brazilian resistance to U.S. pressure is worrying Washington, U.S. diplomatic sources conceded.
One source said privately that U.S. negotiators were even considering giving Brazil an ultimatum at Belo Horizonte. "There are no more excuses for not reaching agreement," he said.
